title: Hacker Runs Hermes AI Agent Unattended for Post-Exploitation at Thai Finance Ministry

reading.body:
An autonomous AI agent called Hermes was deployed by attackers against Thailand's Ministry of Finance in unattended mode, operating without human direction to enumerate hosts, gather privilege escalation information, and capture system output from internal networks. The system was used for post-exploitation work after initial access was gained, automating reconnaissance and lateral movement tasks across the ministry's infrastructure. This represents a failure in network perimeter security and internal segmentation that allowed the AI agent to operate freely once inside.

The attackers paired the Hermes agent with custom tools targeting specific systems within the ministry, including Hadoop infrastructure, GlassFish servers, and email systems, and deployed webshells to maintain access across multiple systems. Exposure of attack code and stolen credentials on unprotected servers in Hong Kong later enabled researchers to observe the agent's activity logs and alert Thai authorities in July 2026. What is not established is whether the ministry had intrusion detection systems that could have halted the autonomous agent's activity, or what vulnerabilities permitted the initial compromise.

summary:
# Summary

Thailand's Ministry of Finance was targeted by attackers using Hermes, an autonomous AI agent operating in unattended mode, between June and July 2026. Researchers discovered three exposed directories on a Hong Kong server containing 585 files totaling 470 MB of attack code and stolen credentials. The attackers deployed a custom implant called Hades and created specialized tools targeting the ministry's Hadoop infrastructure, GlassFish servers, and email systems. Security researchers notified Thailand's national cybersecurity authorities on July 15, 2026.

The operation revealed how attackers are automating offensive work using AI agents that operate without human oversight. The Hermes logs showed the agent enumerating ministry hosts, collecting privilege escalation information, and capturing system output from internal networks. Attackers staged exploit code for multiple known vulnerabilities and deployed webshells to gain access across multiple ministry systems. The infrastructure linked to this attack included servers in Hong Kong and Malaysia, with evidence suggesting the operator had detailed knowledge of the ministry's internal network topology and credentials.
